name: Femi Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly my weeks are a bit chaotic. Mornings are lectures on data structures and discrete maths, afternoons are lab sessions, and evenings I'm usually on my laptop building a small app that helps bakeries plan how much dough to make. My mum runs a bakery back home and my dad teaches secondary school, so that's where the idea came from. I'm in a flat share with four people and I do tutoring for school kids on Sundays for pocket money. I use AI tools for nearly everything, from explaining concepts to reviewing my code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, but I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. At uni I'd say the tools I use every day are already good enough, so if that's the plateau, it's still a big deal for a student. Online I'd probably post that people shouldn't write it off because it isn't magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the safest world for my degree, since the jobs stay and I'm already ahead on the tools. My worry is more about my parents' bakery, because energy prices and flour costs are what hurt them, not AI. If prices carry on rising, Mum might close one of her two shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish my first-year modules, keep building the dough-planner app, and show it to three bakeries in my parents' town this Christmas. I'd keep the Sunday tutoring and try to get a paid summer internship. I'd also try to get my mum to pay a small fee for the app, so it's a real product, not a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own path. A bit knotted when I think of Mum doing 4 am starts at fifty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the dough app meant to become a business or a project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, if I'm honest. For now it's a project, because I get to practise on real data from Mum's shops. If three bakeries pay 15 a month each, it covers my phone and my flat's internet, and that's a real start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plateau is a bit disappointing. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to be part of something big. It's a strange thing to say with my parents' bakery under pressure, but I'd want the tools to help people like Mum. If they plateau at a gadget, it won't fix her margins.

say: Even a **plateau** is a big deal for a student, so don't write it off because it isn't magic.
I'd tell classmates the tools are already **good enough** to matter.
think: This is the **safest world** for my degree, and I'm already ahead on the tools.
My real worry is my parents' **bakery** and rising flour and energy costs.
do: Keep building the **dough-planner app** and show it to three bakeries at Christmas.
Keep the **Sunday tutoring** and apply for a paid summer internship.
Ask my mum to pay a small **fee** so it's a real product.
feel: **Calm** about my own path, knotted about Mum doing 4 am starts.
S0.quote: If three bakeries pay 15 a month each, it covers my phone and my flat's internet, and that's a real start.
fieldNote: Treats the **plateau** as comfortable for himself, since he is already ahead on AI tools.
His worry is the **bakery**: rising costs hit his mum's two shops, not AI.
The dough app is a real **project** with real data, not just an assignment.

steps.text: Show the dough planner to three bakeries at Christmas
Keep Sunday tutoring for school kids
Use AI tools to review my code each evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the most interesting time to study this, but also that we shouldn't leave people behind. In the student group I'd argue for public training funds and for the big models to be more open, instead of owned by three companies. Online I'd post something like a plain explainer, because I like making people less scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think a lot of junior coding work shrinks first, which is exactly what I'm aiming for. But I'm adaptive, so I'd treat it as a game. If I can do the work of a team of three using the tools, I'm more valuable, not less, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on the tools: build a couple of proper projects, learn how to test what the AI writes, and learn some maths properly, since that's what separates people who use tools from people who understand them. I'd also try to get my dad's school to let me run a small coding club. And I'd keep selling the dough app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy, in about equal parts. Like being handed a faster car when the road is full of people who can't drive yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who worries you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's staff, mainly. Her bakery has three part-timers who do the till and the ordering, and software could take over the ordering. Also my dad's pupils, because they'd be applying for office jobs in five years that might not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you build something for them, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. The dough app could do the ordering and let her keep her staff on the shop floor. I'd rather the tool help a small shop than only help a big chain cut headcount.

say: It's the **most interesting** time to study this, but we shouldn't leave people behind.
I'd argue for public training funds and **more open models**, not three owners.
think: Junior **coding work** shrinks first, exactly where I'm headed.
If I can do the work of three people with the tools, I'm **more valuable** for a while.
do: Build a couple of proper projects and learn to **test** what the AI writes.
Learn **maths** properly, since that's what separates users from people who understand.
Run a small **coding club** at my dad's school.
feel: **Excited and uneasy** in equal parts, like a faster car on a road full of new drivers.
S1.quote: I'd rather the tool help a small shop than only help a big chain cut headcount.
fieldNote: Adaptive: treats **disruption** as a game where learning faster pays off.
His **ethic** pulls him towards helping small businesses, not only chasing the best-paid route.
Names the people he worries about: his mum's **part-timers** and his dad's pupils.

steps.text: Build two projects that test AI-written code
Study linear algebra and probability alongside the course
Add ordering features to the dough planner
Back the student group's call for open models

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this changes everything and we need to talk about it properly right now. At uni I'd say the sensible thing is a public push: universal basic income trials, public ownership of the biggest models, and retraining paid for by the companies. I'd say it in the student union, loudly, and I'd be a bit nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared, because it hits exactly the work I'm training for, before I've even got my first real job. It's the one where my adaptability might not be enough, because everyone adapts at once. And my parents: Mum's bakery would suffer, and my dad's school budget would be cut when the council panics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to build something that's mine, whether that's the dough app or another product, so I have something that isn't just a job. I'd keep my degree going, but spend more on projects and networking than on exam grades. I'd also help my parents write a plan for the bakery, like cutting costs and trying automation, before everyone else's shops do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and also kind of buzzing. It's like being at the start of a rollercoaster you can't get off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do the week you heard it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my mum and ask her to send me her real numbers: sales, wages, flour, rent. Then I'd sit down and build her a simple model of what happens if sales drop by a quarter. I'm good with spreadsheets, and the facts are calmer than the fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your own money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd freeze any spending that isn't food or rent. I've got maybe 900 saved from tutoring and summer work, and I'd stop buying new kit. If the degree turns out to be pointless, at least I'd still have a few months of runway.

say: This changes everything, so we need **basic income trials**, public ownership of big models and company-funded retraining.
I'd say it loudly in the **student union**, though I'd be nervous.
think: It hits the work I'm training for before my **first real job**.
Everyone adapts at once, so being **adaptive** might not be enough.
do: Use the two years to build **something that's mine**, like the dough app.
Spend more time on **projects and networking** than on exam grades.
Help my parents write a **bakery plan** with cost cuts and automation.
feel: **Anxious** and buzzing, like the start of a rollercoaster you can't get off.
S2.quote: I'm good with spreadsheets, and the facts are calmer than the fear.
fieldNote: Turns fear into **action**: a spreadsheet model for his mum's bakery.
Recognises that being **adaptive** isn't a plan if everyone adapts at the same time.
Has about **900 saved**, so he sees a few months of runway, not security.

steps.text: Build a product of my own from the dough app
Ask my mum for sales numbers and model a quarter drop
Stop buying new kit and keep to food and rent
Argue for basic income trials in the student union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if we start now, and short enough that nobody can pretend. I'd say it to friends as a kind of challenge: use these years to get really good at the thing machines can't be blamed for, like judgement and making decisions. Online I'd also push the idea that benefits should be shared, not only company profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel almost okay, because I'd be 23 when it lands, with a degree and maybe a small company. It's still a gamble. If the thinking work goes in 2031, I'd want to already own something or have a stake in how it's used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a strong project, and use summers for internships at small firms where I can actually build things. I'd keep growing the dough app, and try to build a proper customer base by graduation. I'd also try to save around 3,000, which is a few months of living costs, so I'm not forced to take a bad job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a bit of dread underneath. Mostly because I'd have enough time to be properly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different from the 2028 one in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'm reacting, and in 2031 I'm choosing. It's the difference between swimming to the shore and swimming in the direction you want. I'd actually spend two years learning how to run a business instead of just a code editor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to work for a company, or on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a bit of both. A job for stability, and a product on the side. It's a way to hedge, because I don't trust any single employer to still need me in 2031.

say: Five years is **enough to prepare** if we start now, and too short for anyone to pretend.
I'd push the idea that **benefits** should be shared, not only company profits.
think: I'd be 23 when it lands, with a degree and maybe a **small company**.
If thinking work goes in 2031, I want to own **something** by then.
do: Use summers for internships at **small firms** where I can build things.
Grow the dough app to a proper **customer base** by graduation.
Save around **3,000** so I'm never forced into a bad job.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a bit of dread, because there's time to be properly ready.
S3.quote: In 2028 I'm reacting, and in 2031 I'm choosing. It's the difference between swimming to the shore and swimming in the direction you want.
fieldNote: The extra years let him go from **reacting** to choosing, and he plans to learn business skills.
Hedges: a **job** for stability with a product on the side, because no employer is trusted to need him in 2031.
Wants to **own** something before thinking work goes.

steps.text: Take summer internships at small software firms
Save 3,000 from tutoring and internship pay
Learn how to run a small business next year
Put dough app income into a company account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd tell people on campus that there's time to rebuild how we train and pay people, and I'd want governments to start now. Online I'd probably be annoyingly positive, but not naive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly relaxed. I'd be 28 by 2036, hopefully with a few years' experience and maybe a company. The more worrying part is the middle years, where the tools get good enough to cut jobs but society hasn't caught up yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a job at a team where I learn how real products get shipped, and try to build my own product in parallel. I'd keep up with the tools every month. And I'd use some of my first salaries to help my parents modernise the bakery, maybe with a better oven or the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious, like planning a long trip. I know there'll be bumps but I've got a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had ten years, what would you do differently from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, less rushing. I'd choose one or two things to get really good at, like building things that people use and explaining them to non-technical people. In 2036, those two skills look to me like the ones that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who is panicking about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's okay to be scared, but make a list. Three skills, three people, three things you'd do if your job vanished. A written plan makes the fear smaller.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if we use it to rebuild how we train and pay people.
Online I'd be annoyingly **positive**, but not naive.
think: I'd be **relaxed**: 28 by 2036 with experience and maybe a company.
The **middle years** worry me, when tools cut jobs before society catches up.
do: Get a job on a team that **ships real products**, and build my own on the side.
Check in on the **tools** every month.
Use early salaries to help my parents **modernise** the bakery.
feel: **Calm and curious**, like planning a long trip with a map.
S4.quote: I'd say it's okay to be scared, but make a list. Three skills, three people, three things you'd do if your job vanished.
fieldNote: Gives **practical** comfort: a written plan of skills, people and fallback actions.
Plans to repay his **parents** by modernising the bakery from his first salaries.
Names the **middle years** as the real danger, not 2036 itself.

steps.text: Join a team that ships real products after graduating
Spend one evening a month testing new AI tools
Keep building my own product on the side
Use early salary to buy my mum a new oven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to turn a plan into reality. Everyone would be adapting at once, so being quick wouldn't set me apart. What would help is public money for retraining that's easy to get, a basic income safety net, and open tools so small shops like my mum's aren't locked out. I'd also want a clear list of which skills hold their value.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd like people to know that students who use the tools every day aren't cheerful about it by default. We're excited and scared together. I'd rather be honest about both than pretend it's all fine or all doom.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be honest about both than pretend it's all fine or all doom.
portrait: Femi is an **18-year-old** software engineering student who uses AI tools daily and builds a dough-planning app for bakeries.
His mum runs a **bakery** and his dad teaches school, so his worries go to their shops, staff and pupils.
He is progressive and wants **public ownership**, open models and basic income, alongside his own side projects.
With time he plans and hedges; with two years he gets **anxious**, since everyone adapts at once.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most: no time to turn a plan into reality, and everyone adapting at once.
whatWouldHelp: Easy **public retraining money**, a basic income safety net, and open tools so small shops aren't locked out.
